findings.summary: handlers package contains 145 files (50% of entire codebase), creating a hub module with excessive blast radius
evidence: internal/handlers contains 145 Go files out of 286 total files (50% of codebase)
handlers package mixes concerns: HTTP handlers, business logic, workers, policies, processors, and domain services
Large files like chatbot_processor.go (92KB), contacts.go (45KB), campaigns.go (47KB) indicate domain logic embedded in handlers
No clear separation between HTTP layer and business logic - handlers directly manipulate models, database, and external services
findings.suggestion: Split handlers into focused packages: handlers/ (HTTP only), services/ (business logic), policies/ (authorization), workers/ (background jobs). Extract domain models from handlers to reduce coupling.

findings.summary: handlers directly import and manipulate internal/models without service layer, creating tight coupling
evidence: Every handler file imports internal/models directly
Handlers contain complex business logic that should be in a service layer (e.g., chat_close_ratings.go has 36KB of rating logic)
No repository pattern or data access layer - handlers use GORM directly on models
Models package is imported by 145+ handler files, creating a large blast radius for model changes
findings.suggestion: Introduce a repository/service layer between handlers and models. Create domain-specific packages (e.g., internal/rating, internal/campaign) that encapsulate business logic and data access.

findings.summary: Two WhatsApp packages (pkg/whatsapp and pkg/whatsmeow) with overlapping responsibilities and unclear boundaries
evidence: pkg/whatsapp has 17 files, pkg/whatsmeow has 67 files - significant size disparity suggests whatsmeow contains domain logic
Both packages implement MessageProvider interface via adapters (whatsapp/adapter.go, whatsmeow/adapter.go)
whatsmeow package contains 67 files with domain logic, connection management, and business rules - not just a thin wrapper
pkg/provider interface is the abstraction boundary, but implementation details leak into both packages
findings.suggestion: Consider consolidating WhatsApp provider logic under a single package with clear internal structure. Move domain-specific whatsmeow logic to internal/whatsmeow if it's not a reusable library.

findings.summary: No init() functions found - all initialization is explicit and controlled
evidence: grep for 'func init()' across entire codebase returned zero results
All initialization happens explicitly in cmd/whatomate/main.go through function calls
Database connections (postgres.go, redis.go) use explicit factory functions (NewPostgres, NewRedis)
Dependencies are injected via App struct constructor in main.go - no global singletons
findings.suggestion: Continue current pattern. The explicit initialization approach is excellent for testability and avoiding boot-order dependencies.

findings.summary: Package-level constants and compiled regexes are safe and appropriate
evidence: Found module-level vars like defaultChatCloseRatingTemplates, localizedRatingDigitReplacer, safeFilenameRe
These are immutable constants compiled at import time - no side effects
No dynamic computation or I/O at module level
All module-level vars are constants, maps, or regex compilations - safe patterns
findings.suggestion: Current patterns are acceptable. Document the immutability contract for package-level variables to prevent future misuse.

findings.summary: handlers package mixes domains without subdirectories, making navigation difficult
evidence: 145 files in single handlers directory - no subdirectories despite clear domain boundaries
Files span multiple domains: accounts, campaigns, chatbot, contacts, organizations, SSO, webhooks, analytics, widgets
No grouping by domain (e.g., handlers/chatbot/*.go, handlers/campaigns/*.go) despite clear domain boundaries
Related files are scattered: chatbot.go, chatbot_processor.go, chatbot_test.go, chatbot_expression_benchmark_test.go are separate files
findings.suggestion: Organize handlers by domain: handlers/accounts/, handlers/campaigns/, handlers/chatbot/, handlers/contacts/. This improves discoverability without adding abstraction layers.

findings.summary: Inconsistent naming between package directories and file purposes
evidence: Some files are entity-focused (contacts.go, accounts.go, organizations.go)
Some files are action-focused (chat_lifecycle.go, send_restriction_policy.go, instance_auto_campaign_worker.go)
Some files are component-focused (activity_middleware.go, template_engine.go, custom_action_runtime.go)
No clear convention for when to use which naming pattern
findings.suggestion: Establish naming convention: entity files for CRUD (contacts.go), feature files for cross-cutting concerns (chat_policy.go), worker files for background jobs (campaign_worker.go). Document this in CONTRIBUTE.md.

findings.summary: Request/Response struct definitions scattered across handler files instead of centralized types package
evidence: Each handler file defines its own Request/Response types (e.g., AccountRequest, CampaignRequest, ContactRequest)
No shared types package for common DTOs
Duplicate patterns across files: every handler has similar Request/Response/Filter structs
Types are not reused across related handlers (e.g., CampaignRequest in campaigns.go but similar types in other files)
findings.suggestion: Create internal/types or internal/dto package for shared request/response structures. Keep handler-specific types in handlers, but extract common patterns.

findings.summary: External dependencies are minimal and appropriate for the domain
evidence: 26 direct dependencies in go.mod - reasonable for a production application
No duplicate functionality (e.g., single HTTP client library, single JWT library)
All dependencies are actively maintained: go-redis/v9, gorm.io/gorm, fasthttp, whatsmeow
No heavy dependencies pulled in for light use - each dep serves a clear purpose
findings.suggestion: Current dependency management is healthy. Consider periodic audits to remove unused dependencies.

findings.summary: whatsmeow dependency pinned to specific commit - good for stability but may miss updates
evidence: go.mau.fi/whatsmeow v0.0.0-20260216124546-34b971e686b6 is pinned to a specific commit
This is appropriate for a library under active development
Pinned version prevents breaking changes from affecting production
However, may miss bug fixes and security updates if not regularly updated
findings.suggestion: Document the update process for whatsmeow dependency. Consider automated dependency scanning to alert on new versions.

findings.summary: handlers package is flat with 145 files, violating the 'flat directory overload' anti-pattern
evidence: 145 files in single directory exceeds 10-file guideline by 14x
Mixed concerns: HTTP handlers, business logic, background workers, policies, utilities
Files range from 600 bytes to 92KB (chatbot_processor.go)
No domain-based subdirectories despite clear domain boundaries (chatbot, campaigns, contacts, accounts, etc.)
findings.suggestion: Reorganize handlers into domain-based subdirectories: handlers/accounts/, handlers/campaigns/, handlers/chatbot/, handlers/contacts/, handlers/analytics/. Keep HTTP handlers in these dirs, move business logic to services/.

findings.summary: pkg/whatsmeow contains 67 files with domain logic, blurring library vs application boundary
evidence: pkg/whatsmeow has 67 files - more than any internal package except handlers
Contains connection management, business logic, adapters, and domain-specific features
pkg/ is intended for reusable libraries, but whatsmeow contains application-specific WhatsApp integration logic
internal/ is for application-private code, but reusable WhatsApp logic lives in pkg/
findings.suggestion: Move whatsmeow application-specific logic to internal/whatsmeow/. Keep only generic whatsmeow wrappers in pkg/ if they're reusable across projects.

findings.summary: Good balance in internal/ packages, but models package is under-structured
evidence: internal/models has 16 files covering all domain models - reasonable size
But models mix concerns: ORM entities, enums, constants, and validation rules
No separation between domain models and database entities (all use GORM annotations)
Models package is imported everywhere, but contains no business logic encapsulation
findings.suggestion: Consider splitting models into: models/ (ORM entities), types/ (domain types), enums/ (constants). This would make dependencies clearer and reduce unnecessary imports.

findings.summary: No internal service or repository layer - handlers directly access models and external services
evidence: Handlers directly use GORM on models (no repository pattern)
Business logic embedded in handlers instead of service layer
No internal/services or internal/domain package despite clear business domains
Cross-cutting concerns (rating logic, campaign logic, chatbot logic) scattered across handler files
findings.suggestion: Introduce internal/services/ package with domain services (e.g., services/campaign, services/rating, services/chatbot). Handlers become thin HTTP adapters that delegate to services.
